solution:
An absolute electrode potential cannot be measured; only the difference between two electrodes can be. So the potential is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), whose potential is fixed at \(0.00\,\text{V}\) at all temperatures by convention.

Set up a galvanic cell at \(298\,\text{K}\) with the SHE as one half-cell and the \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\,|\,\text{Mg}\) system as the other. The SHE is a platinised platinum electrode dipping in \(1\,\text{M}\) \(\text{H}^{+}\) with \(\text{H}_2\) gas bubbled over it at \(1\,\text{bar}\). The other half-cell is a strip of pure magnesium dipping in \(1\,\text{M}\) \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) (say \(\text{MgSO}_4\)) — unit concentration is what makes the measured value the STANDARD potential. Join the two solutions by a salt bridge and connect the electrodes through a voltmeter of very high resistance, so that no appreciable current flows and the reading is the reversible emf.

The voltmeter shows electrons flowing from the magnesium into the external circuit, so magnesium is the anode and the SHE the cathode:

\(\text{Mg}(s)\,|\,\text{Mg}^{2+}(1\,\text{M})\,||\,\text{H}^{+}(1\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{H}_2(1\,\text{bar})\,|\,\text{Pt}(s)\)

Anode: \(\text{Mg}(s) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-}\)

Cathode: \(2\text{H}^{+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_2(g)\)

Since \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode}\) and \(E^{\circ}_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = 0\),

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0 - E^{\circ}_{\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}}\), so \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}} = -E^{\circ}_{(cell)}\).

The measured emf of this cell is \(2.36\,\text{V}\). The minus sign is not arbitrary: it records that magnesium, not the hydrogen electrode, is the electrode at which oxidation occurs, i.e. \(\text{Mg}\) is a stronger reducing agent than \(\text{H}_2\).

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}} = -2.36\,\text{V}\)

No.

From Table 2.1, \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.76\,\text{V}\) and \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\,\text{V}\). The more negative value means zinc is the stronger reducing agent, so zinc metal will reduce \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) out of the solution:

\(\text{Zn}(s) + \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\)

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10\,\text{V}\)

Two electrons are transferred, so \(n = 2\), and with \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\),

\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{(cell)} = -2 \times 96487 \times 1.10 = -2.12 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J mol}^{-1} \approx -212\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

A large negative \(\Delta_r G^{\circ}\) means the displacement is strongly spontaneous. The walls of the pot would dissolve as \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\), a spongy deposit of copper would form on them, and the copper sulphate solution would gradually be converted into zinc sulphate — so both the vessel and the solution would be destroyed.

Copper sulphate solution cannot be stored in a zinc pot.

Oxidising ferrous ion means driving \(\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + e^{-}\), which is the reverse of \(\text{Fe}^{3+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}\), \(E^{\circ} = +0.77\,\text{V}\).

For an oxidant X, \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = E^{\circ}_{\text{X}} - 0.77\,\text{V}\). This is positive (so \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{(cell)}\) is negative) only if the oxidant's own standard reduction potential exceeds \(0.77\,\text{V}\) — that is, only for couples lying ABOVE \(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}\) in Table 2.1.

Three such substances:

1. \(\text{F}_2\), \(E^{\circ} = 2.87\,\text{V}\): \(2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{F}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{F}^{-}\), \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 2.87 - 0.77 = +2.10\,\text{V}\)

2. \(\text{Cl}_2\), \(E^{\circ} = 1.36\,\text{V}\): \(2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{Cl}^{-}\), \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 1.36 - 0.77 = +0.59\,\text{V}\)

3. \(\text{Br}_2\), \(E^{\circ} = 1.09\,\text{V}\): \(2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{Br}^{-}\), \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 1.09 - 0.77 = +0.32\,\text{V}\)

Acidified \(\text{MnO}_4^{-}\) \((1.51\,\text{V})\), acidified \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\) \((1.33\,\text{V})\) and \(\text{O}_2\) in acid \((1.23\,\text{V})\) satisfy the same criterion and will also do it. \(\text{I}_2\) will not, since \(E^{\circ} = 0.54\,\text{V}\) lies below \(0.77\,\text{V}\); on the contrary \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) oxidises \(\text{I}^{-}\).

Three substances that can oxidise \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\): \(\text{F}_2\), \(\text{Cl}_2\) and \(\text{Br}_2\).

The electrode reaction of a hydrogen electrode is

\(2\text{H}^{+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_2(g)\), \(E^{\circ} = 0.00\,\text{V}\), \(n = 2\)

Take the hydrogen gas at the standard pressure \(p_{\text{H}_2} = 1\,\text{bar}\).

Using the Nernst equation in the \(\dfrac{0.059}{n}\log\) form at \(298\,\text{K}\):

\(E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{p_{\text{H}_2}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}} = 0 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.059}{2}\times 2\log[\text{H}^{+}] = 0.059\log[\text{H}^{+}]\)

Since \(\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^{+}]\), this is

\(E = -0.059 \times \text{pH}\)

Substituting \(\text{pH} = 10\):

\(E = -0.059 \times 10 = -0.59\)

Potential of the hydrogen electrode \(= -0.59\,\text{V}\)

The cell reaction is the sum of

Anode: \(\text{Ni}(s) \rightarrow \text{Ni}^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-}\)

Cathode: \(2\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Ag}(s)\)

so two electrons are transferred and \(n = 2\).

The solids \(\text{Ni}\) and \(\text{Ag}\) are at unit activity and do not appear in the reaction quotient, so \(Q = \dfrac{[\text{Ni}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^{2}}\).

Nernst equation at \(298\,\text{K}\), in the \(\dfrac{0.059}{n}\log\) form:

\(E_{(cell)} = E^{\circ}_{(cell)} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\text{Ni}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^{2}}\)

\(= 1.05 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{0.160}{(0.002)^{2}}\)

\(\dfrac{0.160}{4.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 4.0 \times 10^{4}\), and \(\log(4.0 \times 10^{4}) = 4.602\)

\(E_{(cell)} = 1.05 - 0.0295 \times 4.602 = 1.05 - 0.136 = 0.914\)

\(E_{(cell)} = 0.91\,\text{V}\)

The cell reaction is the sum of

Cathode: \(2\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq)\)

Anode: \(2\text{I}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{I}_2(s) + 2e^{-}\)

so two electrons are transferred as written and \(n = 2\).

Standard Gibbs energy, from \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{(cell)}\) with \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\):

\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -2 \times 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1} \times 0.236\,\text{V} = -45542\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

Equilibrium constant, from \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K_c\) at \(298\,\text{K}\):

\(\log K_c = \dfrac{nE^{\circ}_{(cell)}}{0.059} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.236}{0.059} = 8.0\)

\(K_c = 1 \times 10^{8}\)

The same figure follows from \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -RT\ln K\): \(\ln K = \dfrac{45542}{8.314 \times 298} = 18.38\), giving \(K \approx 9.6 \times 10^{7}\).

\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -45.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

\(K_c = 1 \times 10^{8}\)

A metal displaces another metal from the solution of its salt if the first is the stronger reducing agent, i.e. if its standard reduction potential is the more negative. The displacement \(\text{M} + \text{N}^{n+} \rightarrow \text{M}^{n+} + \text{N}\) has \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = E^{\circ}_{\text{N}^{n+}/\text{N}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{M}^{n+}/\text{M}}\), which is positive exactly when \(E^{\circ}_{\text{M}^{n+}/\text{M}}\) is the lower of the two.

From Table 2.1:

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}} = -2.36\,\text{V}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}} = -1.66\,\text{V}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.76\,\text{V}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}} = -0.44\,\text{V}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\,\text{V}\)

So Mg displaces Al, Zn, Fe and Cu; Al displaces Zn, Fe and Cu; Zn displaces Fe and Cu; Fe displaces only Cu; Cu displaces none of them. For example

\(\text{Zn}(s) + \text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Fe}(s)\), \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = -0.44 - (-0.76) = +0.32\,\text{V}\)

while the reverse, \(\text{Fe}(s) + \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq)\), gives \(-0.32\,\text{V}\) and does not occur.

Order in which they displace each other, each metal displacing every metal that follows it:

\(\text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Zn} > \text{Fe} > \text{Cu}\)

Reducing power is the tendency of the metal to lose electrons, \(\text{M} \rightarrow \text{M}^{n+} + ne^{-}\), which is the reverse of the reduction whose potential is quoted. The more negative the standard reduction potential, the greater the reducing power of the metal. Hence arranging the couples from the most positive \(E^{\circ}\) to the most negative gives the metals in INCREASING order of reducing power.

The given values, ordered from most positive to most negative:

\(\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag} = +0.80\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Hg}^{2+}/\text{Hg} = +0.79\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr} = -0.74\,\text{V}\), \(\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg} = -2.37\,\text{V}\), \(\text{K}^{+}/\text{K} = -2.93\,\text{V}\)

Silver, with the highest \(E^{\circ}\), is the poorest reducing agent; potassium, with the lowest, is the best.

Increasing order of reducing power:

\(\text{Ag} < \text{Hg} < \text{Cr} < \text{Mg} < \text{K}\)

In \(\text{Zn}(s) + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s)\) zinc loses electrons and is therefore the anode; silver ion gains them, so the silver electrode is the cathode. Writing the anode on the left, the cell is

\(\text{Zn}(s)\,|\,\text{Zn}^{2+}(aq)\,||\,\text{Ag}^{+}(aq)\,|\,\text{Ag}(s)\)

Physically: a zinc rod dips in \(\text{ZnSO}_4\) solution and a silver rod in \(\text{AgNO}_3\) solution; the two solutions are joined by a salt bridge and the two rods by an external wire through a voltmeter.

With \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}} = +0.80\,\text{V}\) and \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.76\,\text{V}\),

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = 0.80 - (-0.76) = +1.56\,\text{V}\)

so the reaction as written is spontaneous.

(i) The zinc electrode is negatively charged. Oxidation there deposits electrons on the metal, leaving it at the lower potential; it is the negative terminal from which electrons leave into the external circuit.

(ii) Carriers of the current: in the external circuit the current is carried by ELECTRONS, flowing from the zinc electrode to the silver electrode. Inside the cell it is carried by IONS — in the two electrolyte solutions and in the salt bridge, cations moving towards the cathode and anions towards the anode, which keeps both solutions electrically neutral and completes the circuit.

(iii) Individual electrode reactions:

Anode (oxidation): \(\text{Zn}(s) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-}\)

Cathode (reduction): \(\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag}(s)\), which must occur twice for every zinc atom oxidised, i.e. \(2\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Ag}(s)\)

In each case identify the species oxidised (anode) and reduced (cathode), use \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode}\), then \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{(cell)}\) with \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\) and \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K_c\) at \(298\,\text{K}\). The value of \(n\) is the number of electrons transferred in the reaction AS WRITTEN.

(i) \(2\text{Cr}(s) + 3\text{Cd}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+}(aq) + 3\text{Cd}(s)\)

Chromium is oxidised (anode), \(\text{Cd}^{2+}\) is reduced (cathode):

Anode: \(2\text{Cr}(s) \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+}(aq) + 6e^{-}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}} = -0.74\,\text{V}\)

Cathode: \(3\text{Cd}^{2+}(aq) + 6e^{-} \rightarrow 3\text{Cd}(s)\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Cd}^{2+}/\text{Cd}} = -0.40\,\text{V}\)

Six electrons pass, so \(n = 6\).

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = -0.40 - (-0.74) = +0.34\,\text{V}\)

\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -6 \times 96487 \times 0.34 = -196833\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = -196.8\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

\(\log K_c = \dfrac{nE^{\circ}_{(cell)}}{0.059} = \dfrac{6 \times 0.34}{0.059} = 34.58\), so \(K_c = 3.8 \times 10^{34}\)

(ii) \(\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Ag}^{+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{Ag}(s)\)

\(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) is oxidised to \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) (anode), \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) is reduced (cathode):

Anode: \(\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + e^{-}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}} = +0.77\,\text{V}\)

Cathode: \(\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag}(s)\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}} = +0.80\,\text{V}\)

Only one electron passes, so \(n = 1\).

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0.80 - 0.77 = +0.03\,\text{V}\)

\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -1 \times 96487 \times 0.03 = -2895\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = -2.89\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

\(\log K_c = \dfrac{1 \times 0.03}{0.059} = 0.508\), so \(K_c = 3.2\)

(i) \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = +0.34\,\text{V}\), \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -196.8\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(K_c = 3.8 \times 10^{34}\)

(ii) \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = +0.03\,\text{V}\), \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -2.89\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(K_c = 3.2\)
_note: Table 2.1 of this chapter does NOT list the Cd(2+)/Cd couple (it runs Ni -0.25, Fe -0.44, Cr -0.74, Zn -0.76 with no Cd entry). I used the standard tabulated value E(Cd2+/Cd) = -0.40 V and said so in the solution. If the key used a different Cd value, E(cell), dGr and Kc for part (i) all shift accordingly.

solution:
In every case the anode is written on the left of the cell diagram, so \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode}\), and the Nernst equation at \(298\,\text{K}\) is used in the form

\(E_{(cell)} = E^{\circ}_{(cell)} - \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log Q\)

with pure solids and liquids, and gases at \(1\,\text{bar}\), taken at unit activity. Standard potentials are from Table 2.1.

(i) \(\text{Mg}(s)\,|\,\text{Mg}^{2+}(0.001\,\text{M})\,||\,\text{Cu}^{2+}(0.0001\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{Cu}(s)\)

Cell reaction: \(\text{Mg}(s) + \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\), \(n = 2\)

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0.34 - (-2.36) = 2.70\,\text{V}\)

\(E_{(cell)} = 2.70 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\text{Mg}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]} = 2.70 - 0.0295\log\dfrac{0.001}{0.0001}\)

\(= 2.70 - 0.0295 \times 1 = 2.67\,\text{V}\)

(ii) \(\text{Fe}(s)\,|\,\text{Fe}^{2+}(0.001\,\text{M})\,||\,\text{H}^{+}(1\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{H}_2(1\,\text{bar})\,|\,\text{Pt}(s)\)

Cell reaction: \(\text{Fe}(s) + 2\text{H}^{+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\), \(n = 2\)

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0.00 - (-0.44) = 0.44\,\text{V}\)

\(E_{(cell)} = 0.44 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\text{Fe}^{2+}]\,p_{\text{H}_2}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}} = 0.44 - 0.0295\log\dfrac{0.001 \times 1}{(1)^{2}}\)

\(= 0.44 - 0.0295 \times (-3) = 0.44 + 0.0885 = 0.53\,\text{V}\)

(iii) \(\text{Sn}(s)\,|\,\text{Sn}^{2+}(0.050\,\text{M})\,||\,\text{H}^{+}(0.020\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{H}_2(1\,\text{bar})\,|\,\text{Pt}(s)\)

Cell reaction: \(\text{Sn}(s) + 2\text{H}^{+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{2+}(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\), \(n = 2\)

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0.00 - (-0.14) = 0.14\,\text{V}\)

\(E_{(cell)} = 0.14 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\text{Sn}^{2+}]\,p_{\text{H}_2}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}} = 0.14 - 0.0295\log\dfrac{0.050}{(0.020)^{2}}\)

\(\dfrac{0.050}{4.0 \times 10^{-4}} = 125\), and \(\log 125 = 2.097\)

\(= 0.14 - 0.0295 \times 2.097 = 0.14 - 0.062 = 0.078\,\text{V}\)

(iv) \(\text{Pt}(s)\,|\,\text{Br}^{-}(0.010\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{Br}_2(l)\,||\,\text{H}^{+}(0.030\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{H}_2(1\,\text{bar})\,|\,\text{Pt}(s)\)

Here the bromine electrode is written on the left, so it is the anode:

Anode: \(2\text{Br}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Br}_2(l) + 2e^{-}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^{-}} = +1.09\,\text{V}\)

Cathode: \(2\text{H}^{+}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_2(g)\), \(E^{\circ} = 0.00\,\text{V}\)

Cell reaction: \(2\text{Br}^{-}(aq) + 2\text{H}^{+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Br}_2(l) + \text{H}_2(g)\), \(n = 2\)

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0.00 - 1.09 = -1.09\,\text{V}\)

\(E_{(cell)} = -1.09 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{[\text{Br}^{-}]^{2}[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}} = -1.09 - 0.0295\log\dfrac{1}{(0.010)^{2}(0.030)^{2}}\)

\((0.010)^{2}(0.030)^{2} = 9.0 \times 10^{-8}\), so \(Q = 1.11 \times 10^{7}\) and \(\log Q = 7.046\)

\(= -1.09 - 0.0295 \times 7.046 = -1.09 - 0.208 = -1.30\,\text{V}\)

The negative emf means the cell as written is not spontaneous; the reverse reaction, \(\text{Br}_2\) oxidising \(\text{H}_2\), is the spontaneous one.

(i) \(E_{(cell)} = 2.67\,\text{V}\)

(ii) \(E_{(cell)} = 0.53\,\text{V}\)

(iii) \(E_{(cell)} = 0.078\,\text{V}\)

(iv) \(E_{(cell)} = -1.30\,\text{V}\)
_note: For (i) I used Table 2.1's E(Mg2+/Mg) = -2.36 V, giving E(cell) = 2.70 V and E = 2.67 V. The book is internally inconsistent here: the stem of Ex 2.2 quotes Mg2+/Mg = -2.37 V, which would give E(cell) = 2.71 V and E = 2.68 V. The 0.01 V difference is the source of the discrepancy, not the method.

solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: the printed answer is \(1.56\,\text{V}\); for the reaction as written it is \(1.10\,\text{V}\). The key's value is reproduced EXACTLY by a nameable substitution — Table 2.1 prints \(E^{\circ}(\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}) = 0.80\,\text{V}\) and \(E^{\circ}(\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}) = -0.76\,\text{V}\), and \(0.80 - (-0.76) = 1.56\) to the digit — but \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) appears nowhere in this reaction, whose cathode couple is \(\text{Ag}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Ag} + 2\text{OH}^-\) at \(+0.342\,\text{V}\), giving \(0.342 - (-0.762) = 1.104\,\text{V}\). Nor is \(1.56\) the real silver-oxide button cell's voltage, which is about \(1.60\,\text{V}\) and arises from an alkaline \(\text{Zn}/\text{ZnO}\) anode that would contradict the stem's own \(\text{Zn}^{2+}(aq)\) product — so that reading does not rescue it either. There is a second, milder defect behind this one worth knowing: **the \(\text{Ag}_2\text{O}/\text{Ag}\) couple is absent from Table 2.1**, so the chapter supplies no data for its own cathode and a student working strictly from the book cannot reach \(1.104\,\text{V}\) unaided. That is very likely how the key came to use the only silver couple the table does provide.] Split the overall reaction into its half-reactions:

Anode (oxidation): \(\text{Zn}(s) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.76\,\text{V}\) (Table 2.1)

Cathode (reduction): \(\text{Ag}_2\text{O}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Ag}(s) + 2\text{OH}^{-}(aq)\), \(E^{\circ} = +0.344\,\text{V}\)

Adding them reproduces the given reaction \(\text{Zn}(s) + \text{Ag}_2\text{O}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s) + 2\text{OH}^{-}(aq)\), and two electrons pass, so \(n = 2\).

\(E^{\circ} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = 0.344 - (-0.76) = +1.104\,\text{V}\)

Using \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}\) with \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\):

\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -2 \times 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1} \times 1.104\,\text{V} = -213043\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

The cell holds this voltage almost constant through its life because every species in the overall reaction except \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) and \(\text{OH}^{-}\) is a pure solid or liquid, so the reaction quotient barely changes as the cell discharges.

\(E^{\circ} = 1.10\,\text{V}\)

\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -213\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The Ag2O(s) + H2O(l) + 2e- -> 2Ag(s) + 2OH-(aq) couple is NOT in Table 2.1, and the chapter's own button-cell section (Fig. 2.9) describes the MERCURY cell (Zn(Hg) + HgO -> ZnO + Hg, about 1.35 V), not this silver-oxide one. The question therefore supplies no data for the cathode. I used the standard tabulated value +0.344 V and stated it in the solution. If the key used a slightly different value (0.342 or 0.345 V are also tabulated) E and dGr shift by about 0.002 V and 0.4 kJ/mol respectively.

solution:
[Textbook misprint: the question cites \(\text{Table 3.1}\); the standard electrode potentials are in \(\text{Table 2.1}\) of this chapter. The chapter contains no Table 3.x at all — only Tables 2.1 to 2.4 — and this is one of six stale \(3.x\) cross-references surviving from an edition in which Electrochemistry was Unit 3 (the chapter's own QR code still reads 12085CH03). The reference is the only thing broken; the question is answerable as printed.] For each pair, the species with the HIGHER standard reduction potential is the one that gets reduced and the other is oxidised. Then \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode}\), and since \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{(cell)}\), the reaction is feasible (spontaneous) exactly when \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)}\) is positive.

Standard potentials from Table 2.1: \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^{-}} = 1.09\,\text{V}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}} = 0.80\,\text{V}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}} = 0.77\,\text{V}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{I}_2/\text{I}^{-}} = 0.54\,\text{V}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = 0.34\,\text{V}\).

(i) \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) and \(\text{I}^{-}\): \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) is reduced \((0.77\,\text{V})\), \(\text{I}^{-}\) is oxidised \((0.54\,\text{V})\).

\(2\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + 2\text{I}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + \text{I}_2\)

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0.77 - 0.54 = +0.23\,\text{V}\) — feasible.

(ii) \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) and \(\text{Cu}(s)\): \(\text{Ag}^{+}\) is reduced \((0.80\,\text{V})\), \(\text{Cu}\) is oxidised \((0.34\,\text{V})\).

\(2\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + \text{Cu}(s) \rightarrow 2\text{Ag}(s) + \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)\)

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0.80 - 0.34 = +0.46\,\text{V}\) — feasible.

(iii) \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) and \(\text{Br}^{-}\): a reaction would need \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) reduced \((0.77\,\text{V})\) and \(\text{Br}^{-}\) oxidised \((1.09\,\text{V})\).

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0.77 - 1.09 = -0.32\,\text{V}\) — not feasible. \(\text{Br}_2\) is the stronger oxidising agent, so the reverse reaction is the spontaneous one.

(iv) \(\text{Ag}(s)\) and \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\): a reaction would need \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) reduced \((0.77\,\text{V})\) and \(\text{Ag}\) oxidised \((0.80\,\text{V})\).

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0.77 - 0.80 = -0.03\,\text{V}\) — not feasible.

(v) \(\text{Br}_2(aq)\) and \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\): \(\text{Br}_2\) is reduced \((1.09\,\text{V})\), \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) is oxidised \((0.77\,\text{V})\).

\(\text{Br}_2(aq) + 2\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{Br}^{-}(aq) + 2\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq)\)

\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 1.09 - 0.77 = +0.32\,\text{V}\) — feasible.

(i) Feasible, \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = +0.23\,\text{V}\)

(ii) Feasible, \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = +0.46\,\text{V}\)

(iii) Not feasible, \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = -0.32\,\text{V}\)
